messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Marking header functions as inline
parts:
Marcus, do you have a reference explaining what's the right thing to do? Searching for those terms don't really return anything useful in Google.



Daniel


On Mon, Nov 24, 2014 at 2:12 PM, Marcus Brubaker <notifi...@github.com> wrote:
Based on the function mentioned I suspect the issue is not with templating,
but rather with some of the non-templated functions used as helpers. For
instance, see stan/prob/internal_math.hpp which defines a number of
non-templated functions which really should be marked as inline or compiled
into an object file.

Marius, the issue is that Stan only ever has a single translation unit (a
single model) so these issues have never really come up for us. Fixing it
shouldn't be too hard and a pull request which simply added inline to a
bunch of functions would likely be quickly reviewed.

wrote:

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Marking header functions as inline
parts:
Building a model still involves linking the libstan.a archive,
which makes up its own translation unit.

Building the parser involves multiple translation units so that
the Windows compilers and assemblers don't choke on all the templates.

Daniel --- Searching for what terms? Declaring a function inline
lets you define it in multiple translation units --- that's its
only real effect. Member functions (non-static functions in classes)
are automatically inline (I don't know about statics).

The "please unfold my code" part of the inline declaration is just
a suggestion to the compiler, which can do whatever it damn well
pleases as long as it obeys what passes for a spec for C++ (I hate
that so much is platform dependent and can thus vary among compilers
or optimization levels).

I didn't see the original query from Marius.

- Bob

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: Marking header functions as inline
parts:
Well, if you look at the functions in the mentioned file, you'll see that they're basic, non-templated functions.  E.G., consider a foo.hpp which has:

void foo(double x, double y) {
...
}

if there are two cpp files that include foo.hpp, say a.cpp and b.cpp that get compiled separately and linked together:

g++ -c -o a.o a.cpp
g++ -c -o b.o b.cpp
g++ -o runme a.o b.o

Then the final compilation to runme will produce an error because the symbol foo was compiled and produced a symbol in both a.o and b.o and these conflict when they're linked together.

The solution (which keeps Stan mostly header-only) is to mark foo() as inline so the compiler doesn't generate a symbol for it in a.o and b.o.  You can also remove the definition of foo from the header and put it into a cpp file of it's own which is compiled separately and linked, but this would complicate model building and would do practically nothing for our compile times since these functions are (as far as I can tell) a very small part of the code base.

Cheers,
Marcus
